concepts.def: Designing products so they are simpler and cheaper to make, by minimising part counts, using standard components and realistic tolerances.
Designing parts that locate themselves, fit only the correct way and need few fasteners, reducing assembly time, errors and labour cost.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Design For Manufacturing & Project Management — a core area of A-Level Design Technology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Design For Manufacturing & Project Management brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Design For Manufacturing & Project Management.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: What does a Gantt chart display?
options: Project tasks plotted against time
The forces acting on a structure
The chemical composition of a material
A product's retail price history

mcqs.q: What is the critical path of a project?
options: The longest sequence of dependent tasks, setting the minimum project duration
The list of the most hazardous tasks
The route materials take through the factory
The cheapest possible order of tasks

mcqs.q: Which change best illustrates design for manufacture?
options: Reducing the number of separate components in a product
Adding decorative features to impress customers
Specifying the tightest tolerance on every dimension
Using a unique custom screw for each fixing

mcqs.q: What is a go/no-go gauge used for?
options: Quickly checking that a dimension lies within tolerance
Measuring the exact hardness of a material
Timing tasks on the critical path
Counting components in a kit

mcqs.q: What is the difference between quality control and quality assurance?
options: QC and QA are the same thing — checking products at the end of the line.
Quality control inspects and tests outputs against tolerances; quality assurance is the whole system of procedures designed to prevent defects occurring in the first place.
QA stands for 'quick assembly' of standard parts.
The critical path is the conveyor route through the factory.

mcqs.q: Should designers always specify the tightest possible tolerance?
options: No — tighter tolerances require more precise machinery and inspection, raising cost; good practice specifies the loosest tolerance that still guarantees function.
Tolerance describes how well a material resists heat.
Tighter tolerances always mean a better, more professional design.
The critical path is the conveyor route through the factory.

mcqs.q: What does the critical path in a project plan show?
options: The critical path is the conveyor route through the factory.
The critical path lists the tasks that are most dangerous and need safety checks.
QA stands for 'quick assembly' of standard parts.
The longest chain of dependent tasks, which fixes the minimum project duration; any delay on this path delays the entire project.

free_texts.hint: Allows failed parts to be swapped.

sequence.def: Project starts by stating the problem, users and constraints
Measurable criteria are drawn up from the brief before designing
Tasks and deadlines are mapped before development work begins
Design is proved to work before money is spent on production
Production equipment is built once the design is frozen
Manufacture runs at volume, checked against the specification
